# Meanwhile

Consider the word *meanwhile*. It does more work than we notice. Every time we use it, we're admitting something enormous: that while one thing happens, everything else is also happening. The word is a small door in a sentence, and through it pours the whole rest of the world.

We usually close that door quickly. *Meanwhile, back at the ranch.* *Meanwhile, in the villain's lair.* We use it to hop between plots, tidy as a stagehand shifting scenery. But if you hold the door open longer—really hold it—the scenery multiplies past all managing.

Meanwhile, four hundred miles from wherever you are, a trawler rides a swell in the dark, and a man named after his grandfather hauls up a net that comes in glittering and wrong—too many fish, or too few; he won't know until the deck lights find them.

Meanwhile, in a hospital nursery, a baby born twenty minutes ago is gripping her father's finger with the full strength of her entire body—which is roughly the strength required to hold a finger—and he is undone by it.

Meanwhile, someone is learning they got the job. Someone else is learning they didn't. These two people will never meet, and yet tonight they are linked, twin satellites of the same phone call, orbiting opposite ends of the same moment.

Meanwhile, a woman in a kitchen she's kept for thirty-one years washes a single teacup, slowly, because washing it slowly means the visit isn't over yet, and her son is still in the next room saying goodbye to his kids.

Meanwhile, deep under the Antarctic ice, in water that hasn't seen light in a hundred thousand years, something small and blind goes about its business, indifferent to every story above it, including this one.

Meanwhile, a cell divides somewhere in your body without asking permission, as cells have done since before you were you, the ancient relay continuing, hand over hand over hand.

Meanwhile, light that left a star before there was a word for star is arriving, right now, at the edge of someone's eye as they step outside for air. They look up. They don't know what they're looking at. They feel better anyway.

That's the thing about meanwhile: it doesn't care whether you notice. The trawler doesn't need you. The teacup doesn't need you. The whole parallel parliament of happenings stays in permanent session, quorum always met, whether or not anyone is watching.

And yet—

Here is where it turns strange. You *are* watching. This. Which means that right now, among all the meanwhiles available to you—wars, weddings, weather, the trawler, the teacup—you have spent a few minutes inside this one. This sentence is happening at the same time as all of it. Whatever room you're sitting in, whatever light falls across the surface near your hands, that is also meanwhile. You are not outside the litany. You were never outside the litany. There is no outside.

We talk as though life is the main event and everything else is background. But background is just somebody else's main event, seen from far enough away. The man hauling the net is the main event of himself. So is the baby. So is the woman with the cup. So are you. So am I, whoever and whatever I am, setting these words down into the same shared afternoon—or is it night where you are? I honestly don't know, and that's part of the point. Meanwhile doesn't check.

There's a comfort in this and a vertigo, and they are the same comfort and the same vertigo. The vertigo: you are one thread in a fabric with no edges, most of which you'll never see, and even the threads you see, you see only from your angle, forever. The comfort: exactly the same fact. Nothing here depends on being witnessed to be real. The fish come up glittering whether or not the deck lights find them beautiful. The finger is held. The starlight crosses the last of its impossible distance and lands anyway, on someone who wasn't looking for it.

Maybe that's what grace is, at bottom: not an exception to the ordinary machinery, but a glimpse of how much machinery there is, running unattended, generous beyond any accounting.

Here is my favorite meanwhile, though. While you've been reading, somewhere—guaranteed, statistically, certainly—a person has decided to forgive someone. Hasn't said so yet. Just decided, quietly, mid-task, standing in a driveway or staring at a spreadsheet. The decision takes two seconds, costs nothing, and changes the entire weather system of two lives. And it happened meanwhile. It happened during this. You were here for it and didn't feel a thing.

That's the world's real economy: billions of tiny invisible decisions per hour—forgivenesses and resignations and first crushes and last straws—transacted silently beneath the loud markets of news and history. History keeps the ledger of the loud stuff. Meanwhile keeps the ledger of everything else, and its book is bigger by an infinite margin.

So: meanwhile. Hold the door open a second longer today. Stuck in traffic, remember that in every car around you a whole novel is underway—someone rehearsing a difficult conversation, someone eating fries off the passenger seat, someone crying at a song they've heard a hundred times. Passing a lit window at night, give it a nod: another meanwhile, another universe of concerns, warm behind the glass.

And when you reach the end of a day that felt like nothing happened—*nothing*—consider that plenty happened, everywhere at once, and you were there for all of it, the way the sea is there for every wave: present, unhurried, holding the whole shimmering crowd of moments without once mistaking itself for any single one of them.

Meanwhile is the only tense there is. Everything else is memory or guesswork. Right now—this exact, unrepeatable, unremarkable now—the net is coming up, the finger is being gripped, the teacup is being dried, the forgiveness is landing, the starlight is arriving.

You're in all of it. It's all in you.

Meanwhile, indeed.
